  "text": "The clock above the laundrette dryers had been eleven minutes slow for as long as Nina could remember. Her father said people waiting for washing weren’t going anywhere.

“Some of them are,” she said.

He was sorting coins into paper sleeves. He pushed a stack towards her without answering.

Nina came after college on Thursdays. She used to bring homework, but the folding table was usually wet.

One evening, a woman in a green coat asked whether she could leave her sheets while she collected her son.

“Back by six,” Nina’s father said.

The woman looked at the clock.

“Proper six,” Nina added.

After she had gone, Nina fetched the stepladder from behind the mop bucket.

“Battery’s fine,” her father said.

“I know.”

The clock left a pale circle on the wall. Nina turned the little wheel at the back, checked her phone, then moved the minute hand again.

Her father watched from the counter.

“It’ll only lose time.”

“Then we’ll know how much.”

At six, the woman hadn’t returned. Her sheets sat folded in a blue bag.

Nina put on her jacket.

“You go,” her father said. “I’ve got the till.”

From the bus stop across the road, she saw him unlock the door for the woman and carry the bag out to her car.

The following Thursday, the clock showed the right time. Beneath it, on the counter, lay a packet of batteries with one missing.

“Your tea’s by the sink,” her father said.

Nina took her books to the folding table. He had wiped it dry."
